newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ tankan forecasts mixed, rates on hold.
newsitem.headline: BOJ tankan forecasts mixed, rates on hold.

text.p: The Bank of Japan will likely keep interest rates on hold for a while longer, whatever the results of a key central bank survey of business sentiment due out next week, most economists polled by Reuters say.

"The Bank of Japan will not be able to confirm the economic recovery with this survey, so there is not likely to be a change in monetary policy," said Haruki Kawano, chief economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd.

Markets are keen to see the data in the Bank of Japan's quarterly survey of corporate sentiment, known as the "tankan," on June 25 for clues to when the central bank will tighten its hyper-easy credit policy.

Forecasts vary for the closely watched diffusion index (DI) for manufacturers -- an important guide to corporate sentiment -- with some economists expecting companies to have grown somewhat cheerier and others predicting a return to gloom.

Forecasts for the manufacturers' DI at 16 think tanks averaged at about zero, but ranged from minus four to plus four. That compared to plus two in March, when the last survey was conducted and when the tankan forecast a manufacturers' DI of minus one in June.
The index represents the percentage of companies which see business conditions as favourable minus the percentage of those which see conditions as unfavourable.

Those expecting manufacturers to have grown rather more pessimistic cited the dampening effect of government fiscal tightening and a rise in the national consumption tax to five percent from three percent from April 1 as the key factors, along with the yen's recent rise against the dollar.
Others, however, said the yen's appreciation was likely to have done little damage to manufacturers' competitive edge.

"Our view is that while the yen has appreciated somewhat, manufacturers are still competitive and with inventories low...the outlook is not so bad," said Ron Bevacqua, an economist at Merrill Lynch Japan.

A large gap in sentiment between nimble manufacturers and their laggard and gloomier non-manufacturing colleagues as well as between bigger and smaller firms, highlighted in the March tankan, probably persists. Some economists, however, said the gap may have narrowed as non-manufacturers benefited from lower import costs on the back of the yen's rise.

"Basically, we think it's a Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde economy, with a very strong manufacturing sector getting a further boost from low interest rates, which weaken the currency, at the same time that non-manufacturers haven't restructured and continue to see their operating margins shrink," said Andrew Shipley, an economist at Schroders Japan.

Forecasts for the non-manufacturers' diffusion index ranged from minus 10 to minus three, compared to an actual minus six in March, when the tankan forecast an index of minus seven for June. The average forecast was about minus six.

Whatever their tankan expectations, few economists foresee an early rise in interest rates, which have rested at rock bottom levels since the BOJ slashed its official discount rate to an historic low of 0.5 percent in September 1995.

Most expect the central bank to wait until autumn or even later for more data -- including a probable cheerier September tankan -- to make sure that the recovery is on track and give the bad loan-laden financial sector further breathing space.
"Why should these guys be in a hurry?" said Russell Jones at Lehman Brothers. "I don't think there is any incentive to move at this time."
But a few believe the central bank could move more quickly.
Susumu Kato, chief economist at BZW Securities, thinks the Bank of Japan could raise its official discount rate as early as August or September by 50 basis points.

"Naturally, the business cycle fluctuates short-term but monetary policy is based on the long-term growth trend and if that is confirmed, the current record low rates could be adjusted," Kato said. "Rates are at an inappropriately low level."
